articles.title: In 2024, Martin County voters approved a half-cent sales tax for conservation; two years later more than 2,000 acres are protected and eight more properties are being pursued
articles.summary: US News: In 2024, voters in Martin County, Florida, approved a half-cent sales tax dedicated to conservation, betting that a small, broad-based levy could prot.
articles.body: In 2024, voters in Martin County, Florida, approved a half-cent sales tax dedicated to conservation, betting that a small, broad-based levy could protect the natural landscapes that define their communities. Just two years later, that decision is already reshaping the county’s map. More than 2,000 acres of wetlands, forests and wildlife habitat have been permanently protected, and county officials are actively pursuing eight additional properties for acquisition. As reported by Martin County Forever and local news outlets, the program is moving quickly from ballot measure to on-the-ground results, with new preserves opening to the public and more deals in the pipeline.A voter-backed mandate for land protectionThe Martin County Forever initiative was placed on the ballot to address growing concerns about development pressure, habitat fragmentation and water-quality threats in one of Florida’s most ecologically rich counties. The half-cent sales tax generates a steady stream of local funding that can be used to: Purchase conservation easements or full ownership of key parcels; restore degraded habitats such as wetlands, pine flatwoods and mangrove forests; and provide public access for low-impact recreation like hiking, birding and paddling.Because the funding comes from a sales tax rather than property taxes, it spreads the cost across residents and visitors while creating a dedicated revenue source that is harder to divert to other uses.More than 2,000 acres locked inWithin two years of the tax’s approval, Martin County has already secured protection for more than 2,000 acres of land. These acquisitions include a mix of large, contiguous blocks and smaller but strategically important parcels that connect existing preserves or buffer sensitive waterways.Some of the protected lands are being managed as new county preserves, with trails, interpretive signage and parking areas designed to welcome the public while minimising ecological impact. Others are held as conservation easements, where private owners retain title but agree to permanent restrictions on development, ensuring the land remains forested, farmed or in its natural state.Eight more properties in the pipelineCounty officials say the early acquisitions are just the beginning. According to recent reporting, Martin County is now eyeing the purchase of eight additional properties, which could add thousands more acres to the protected network if deals are completed.These targets were chosen based on criteria such as:High ecological value, including rare habitats or critical wildlife corridors.Proximity to existing preserves, allowing for larger, more resilient conservation areas.Opportunities to protect water quality by buffering rivers, estuaries and recharge zones.Potential for public access and outdoor recreation that aligns with the county’s vision for nature-based tourism.Negotiations are ongoing, and not every targeted parcel is guaranteed to be acquired, but the county’s active pursuit signals a clear intent to build on the initial momentum.How the money is being spentThe Martin County Forever program is overseen by a citizen advisory committee that reviews potential projects and makes recommendations to the Board of County Commissioners. The county’s Land Acquisition office manages appraisals, negotiations, closings and long-term stewardship of the properties.Funds are being used for: Land purchases and conservation easements; habitat restoration, such as removing invasive plants, replanting native species and restoring natural hydrology; basic infrastructure for public access, including trails, boardwalks, parking and signage; and ongoing management and monitoring to ensure the lands deliver lasting conservation benefits.The county publishes regular updates on projects, maps and spending, allowing residents to track how their tax dollars are being used.Why Martin County’s landscape mattersMartin County sits at the heart of the Treasure Coast, where the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon meet the Atlantic Ocean. The area supports a rich mix of habitats, including mangrove forests, seagrass beds, freshwater marshes, pine flatwoods and hardwood hammocks. These ecosystems provide critical services: filtering water, storing floodwaters, supporting fisheries and offering refuge for wildlife such as manatees, sea turtles, wading birds and the Florida panther.At the same time, the county faces intense development pressure from population growth, tourism and infrastructure projects. Without strategic protection, key parcels can be lost to subdivision, paving and drainage changes that fragment habitat and degrade water quality. The Martin County Forever tax is designed to counter that trend by giving the county a reliable tool to compete in the real estate market and lock in conservation before it’s too late.Public access and community benefitsOne of the selling points of the program is that many of the protected lands will be open to the public for low-impact recreation. New preserves and trail systems are being designed to connect residents and visitors with nature while generating economic benefits for nearby communities.Activities planned or already available include: Hiking and nature walks on designated trails; birdwatching and wildlife viewing from boardwalks and observation platforms; paddling access to rivers, creeks and mangrove tunnels; and educational programs for schools and community groups focused on local ecology and conservation.By tying conservation to recreation and education, the county aims to build broad, lasting support for the program.A model for other Florida countiesMartin County’s rapid progress is drawing attention from other parts of Florida, where similar half-cent or penny sales taxes have been used for conservation, parks and infrastructure. The combination of voter approval, clear criteria and transparent reporting is seen as a blueprint for how local governments can turn conservation goals into tangible results.For now, the focus remains on finishing current acquisitions, advancing the eight properties in negotiation and ensuring that the lands already protected are well managed for the long term. If the early pace continues, Martin County could add thousands more acres to its protected network in the coming years, reshaping both its landscape and its legacy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tiny Scottish village of 200 homes in Auchtertool, Fife, fights plans for world’s second-largest data centre covering more than 100 football pitches; 1,600 objections pile up, residents fear it could dwarf their community
articles.summary: UK News: Residents of a tiny Scottish village have launched a fierce campaign against plans to build what has been described as the world's second-largest data.
articles.body: Residents of a tiny Scottish village have launched a fierce campaign against plans to build what has been described as the world's second-largest data centre on their doorstep.The proposed Cato data centre in Auchtertool, Fife, would occupy a site larger than 100 football pitches and sit next to a village of around 200 homes.Locals fear the huge development could fundamentally change the character of their community, with concerns ranging from noise and light pollution to flooding, environmental impact and the potential effect on animals.More than 1,600 objections have reportedly been submitted against the plans, while protest banners have appeared outside homes, in the village park and on residents' cars.For many people living in Auchtertool, however, the debate is about more than a major infrastructure project. They fear losing the quiet rural life they chose when they moved to the village.‘Our peace is being threatened’Speaking to the Daily Mail, Fiona Stewart, 53, who lives at Wilmar Cottage overlooking the proposed site, said she was shocked when she first saw the scale of the development.“When I saw the scale and size of the planned data centre I was horrified. It's bigger than the village and right next to it,” she said.Stewart stressed that she was not opposed to data centres in principle and understood why they were needed in an increasingly digital world.“But I don't know how you can ever justify putting them in a site next to a tiny village,” she added.Her concerns include light pollution, noise and flooding, particularly because parts of the area have previously flooded during periods of heavy rain.“I'm worried about light pollution. I'm worried about the noise that comes from them, worried about the flood risk,” she said.“It's not like I'm against progress. We're calling on the First Minister to just pause this, take a look at the plan and the framework, and make sure that these are regulated properly.”The strength of feeling has already prompted residents to prepare for a demonstration at Holyrood on September 3, alongside communities elsewhere in Scotland facing similar data centre proposals.‘We chose to live here for the quiet life’For Clare Williams, 51, who has lived in the area for nine years, the proposed development threatens something much more personal: the tranquillity of her home.The foster carer has put up a protest banner outside her house and said residents were initially given one impression of the proposed buildings' height before being told they could be significantly taller.Williams said the potential scale of the development, as well as concerns about heat and noise, had left her deeply worried.“I've done the party life and I chose to live here for the quiet life,” she said.“We are in the countryside. And it's quiet. My mum comes here and when she sits in the garden, she loves it. It's just so peaceful and serene and you can sit outside and just hear the birds, but our peace is being threatened.”She added: “I'm angry, frustrated, worried, stressed, all of that.”Williams is also concerned about the potential impact on property values.“We have spent money on living here and wouldn't be able to afford to sell up if it happens because the house wouldn't be worth what it is,” she said.“People will lose potentially hundreds of thousands on their properties. We need more information.”Her objection, she insists, is not rooted in opposition to artificial intelligence or technology.“It's not like I'm anti-AI and I'm not anti-data centres. But how many do we need? Do we need to have them on people's doorsteps?”Her message to the developers is blunt: “Please reconsider and look at alternatives.”Why are residents concerned about the data centre?Data centres are large facilities designed to store, process and manage huge quantities of digital information. They are an increasingly important part of the infrastructure supporting cloud computing, artificial intelligence, online services and the wider internet.Scotland is attracting interest from the data centre industry because of its renewable energy resources and electricity infrastructure.But the rapid expansion of AI and cloud computing has also intensified debate over the environmental footprint of such facilities, including their energy consumption, water requirements, cooling systems, noise and impact on surrounding communities.In Auchtertool, residents say the sheer scale of the proposed development is at the heart of their concerns.Andrea Cail, chair of the community council, said locals first became aware of the proposal around March 2025.“We were concerned by the proposal because of the sheer size of the buildings [and] the site, because it's just at the top end of the village, and it's on agricultural land,” she said.At the time, Cail said, residents knew little about the data centre industry.“We knew very little about data centres at that point, but we twigged that it was going to be quite energy rich, and it would need a lot of electricity, and it would probably need a lot of water.”The facility would operate around the clock, she said, raising questions about its long-term impact on the surrounding community.“We know it's a 24/7 facility, and once it's up and running, it won't just hum. It will make quite a bit of noise. We don't know what the longer term effects might be.”Environmental impact assessment becomes key issueOne of the major developments in the dispute concerns the environmental assessment of the project.According to Cail, Fife Council was initially asked to carry out screening to determine whether a full environmental impact assessment was required. She said the council initially determined that one was not necessary.However, the Scottish Government has since requested that a full Environmental Impact Assessment be carried out.For campaigners, the decision has provided some encouragement after months of frustration.“I'm frustrated. I've gone through being angry, very frustrated, but also slightly cheered, because last week, the Scottish Government decreed that there had to be a full environmental impact assessment done on this planning application,” Cail said.She said campaigners had also been working with communities elsewhere in Scotland that were facing similar proposals.“They've picked here because we have good grid connections and they will be able to get the electricity they require,” she said.Horse owners fear impact on animalsAmong the most anxious residents are Adele and Russell Seeth, who live at Glenniston Farm Cottage, close to where the proposed development would begin.The couple are particularly concerned about the potential impact on their horses and other animals.They say they were not included in some of the correspondence relating to the proposed development because their farm sits on the boundary of the site.Russell Seeth, who has lived at the property for 23 years, said the family had already experienced the arrival of several large renewable-energy projects in the surrounding area.“We've had the wind turbines. They told us that wasn't going to make any noise, and it makes noise,” he said.“We've had the battery storages and 98,000 solar panels going around us, ten metres off the fence line... but when we saw this data centre, it was like, ‘wow’.”The couple said they were particularly concerned about their three horses, which they describe as high-performance British showjumping animals.Russell said the proposed facility's round-the-clock cooling systems and emergency generators could create a challenging environment for the animals.“There's a real concern to us that there will be acoustic shock to them,” he said.“They're highly strung flight-sensitive athletes. The 24/7 low-frequency hum from massive industrial cooling fans, and sudden testing of emergency diesel backup generators, present a severe psychological and physical threat to their welfare and training.”Adele said the horses would be only around 270 metres from the proposed site.“Our daughters do British showjumping, so we put in the arena here a few years back to allow them to train here and ride here,” she said.“Their whole life is going to be disturbed and changed if this happens.”The couple have also cited concerns about the potential increase in local temperatures and have pointed to reports about the environmental impact of large data centres elsewhere.However, claims about specific temperature increases and alleged animal-health effects from other developments remain matters for scientific and environmental assessment rather than established consequences of the Auchtertool proposal.Developers say the project will bring jobs and investmentILI Group, the developer behind the Cato proposal, has defended the plans and said it understands the strength of feeling within the community.Mark Wilson, CEO of ILI Group, said the project was subject to the planning process and had already undergone technical assessments covering issues including noise, air quality, water, landscape and ecology.“Noise assessments we have undertaken show the project can operate within acceptable limits,” Wilson said, adding that the company welcomed the Scottish Government's decision to require a full Environmental Impact Assessment.He also urged people to judge the proposal on the development actually being put forward rather than comparing it directly with data centres elsewhere in the world.“Comparisons with data centre developments elsewhere in the world do not necessarily reflect the design, technology, environmental standards or regulatory requirements that would apply to this proposal in Scotland,” he said.According to ILI Group, the built development would occupy only a small portion of the wider site, while plans also include new woodland, wetland and meadow habitat.The developer says the project could also deliver significant economic benefits to Fife.Independent analysis by BiGGAR Economics, cited by ILI Group, estimates the project could support around 1,450 job-years during construction and approximately 262 jobs in Fife once operational, including around 120 permanent on-site positions.“We are committed to continuing to engage constructively with the local community as the environmental assessment progresses, listening to concerns and providing clear, evidence-based information about the proposals,” Wilson said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: D4vd legal team abruptly withdraws, singer taps public defender for murder trial
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — D4vd and his legal team parted ways with the singer opting instead to be represented by public defenders in his high-profile murder case, he told a stunned Los Angeles courtroom on Monday.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — D4vd and his legal team parted ways with the singer opting instead to be represented by public defenders in his high-profile murder case, he told a stunned Los Angeles courtroom on Monday. After lawyers had met with L.A. County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo in chambers, defense attorney Blair Berk emerged and told the court that her client, whose real name is David Burke, wants the public defender. “Is that your wish, Mr. Burke,” Judge Olmedo asked. The defendant responded, “Yes.” The surprising turnaround came during what normally would have been a routine pre-trial hearing in this case, in which D4vd is accused of killing a 14-year-old girl, whose decaying remains were found in the trunk of his abandoned car. D4vd’s new attorney, Walid Fouad Kandeel, had been seated in the gallery until Berk disclosed the change of legal teams. Judge Olmedo then asked the public defender to step forward and introduce himself to the court. The defendant’s new counsel asked for Monday’s arraignment to be continued to give him more time to study the case. The judge denied that request before entering not guilty pleas on behalf of the defendant, promising to give Kandeel more time to prepare if he needed it. Olmedo then ordered all parties to return to court on Oct. 19. The defendant, shackled and wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, smiled and shook hands with his now-former attorneys Berk and Regina Peter as court was adjourned. Burke will remain held in custody without bail. “This morning the court granted our request to withdraw as counsel and appoint the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office after it was determined David qualified for appointed counsel,” according to a statement from Berk. “We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges. We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him.” The Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office extended its condolences to the victim’s loved ones. “We recognize the loss of life underlying the allegations and extend our sympathies to those who are grieving,” the office said in a statement. “At the same time, David Burke is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence. We are committed to providing him with that defense.” It wasn’t immediately clear why Burke and his lawyers separated. “I’m sure the Public Defender will give him a zealous representation,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said. Judge Olmedo back on July 27 had ordered the 21-year-old artist to stand trial after prosecutors presented evidence at a preliminary hearing in connection to the slaying of Celeste Rivas Hernandez. Burke was arrested on the afternoon of April 16 at a house on Marmont Avenue in the Hollywood Hills, Los Angeles police said. Beack on Sept. 8 of last year, police found the remains of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, in the trunk of a Tesla impounded at Hollywood Tow. Officers were drawn the scene after reports of a foul odor coming from the vehicle. Text messages between Hernandez and the defendant say she had gotten pregnant at age 13 and had an abortion. And in one exchange between the girl and the suspect in early January 2024, Burke apologized for “putting her through this.” Madeline Morrison reported from Los Angeles and David K. Li from New York City.

articles.title: Ukraine racing to develop new interceptors as Russian drones and missiles ravage the country
articles.summary: Ukraine is urgently trying to develop interceptors capable of countering a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones that have wreaked havoc across the country in recent months.
articles.body: Ukraine is urgently trying to develop interceptors capable of countering a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones that have wreaked havoc across the country in recent months. Along with the Kremlin’s ballistic weapons and a new type of cruise missile, the jet-drones have caused massive damage in and around the capital, Kyiv. They have also been used to target warehouses, gas stations, postal facilities and factories in what is becoming a much broader war in terms of targets. The jet-powered Shahed drones – known as the Geran-4 and Geran-5 – are more difficult to intercept because of their speed and number. They are three times faster than the original Shaheds that Russia procured from Iran. “Drone attacks are constant, with many jet-powered Shaheds,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday. Almost 1,500 drones of all types were fired at Ukraine over the previous four days, more than half of them jet-powered, he said. The mass deployment of the jet-powered drones has accelerated over the past two months. About 1,500 were used in July, and more than 2,500 in August, according to Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky . They were “being launched at Ukraine practically straight from the factory,” he said in a Facebook post at the weekend. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence alleges that the jet-powered drones contain hundreds of components made by foreign companies, including in the US, UK and China. Many of the jet-powered drones have been fired at the capital as Russia has moved to barrages against Kyiv both day and night. On Saturday, the Ukrainian military said Russia fired 224 drones at Ukraine in daylight hours – most of them jet-powered. On Sunday, Kyiv experienced eight air raid alerts between midnight and dusk. The Kremlin’s goal is to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses and sap the morale of civilians, as it expands its list of targets to food warehouses and stores and continues strikes against energy infrastructure, say Ukrainian officials. “The enemy is trying to paralyze economic activity in the capital and major cities, so our approaches and response mechanisms must change,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said over the weekend. The intensity of Russian daytime strikes also comes just as children are preparing for the new school year. The Kyiv city office said Monday it was likely that lessons will be disrupted and urged parents to discuss with their children “some simple yet important issues – how they should act in the event of an alert, where they should take shelter, and what they should do if they are caught in a dangerous situation on their way to school.” “In the current circumstances, this is just as much a part of preparing for the new school year as packing a school bag or getting the school uniform ready,” it said. The Chess Game of Innovation For now, Zelensky has acknowledged, it is mainly combat aircraft that protect against the jet-powered drones. But Ukraine’s small air force is already stretched, and using fighter jets against the drones is expensive. And so the race is on in yet another episode of the leapfrog technology race that has characterized the nearly five-year war. Four companies have developed relevant interceptor drones, one of which had “the most successful technology,” Zelensky said on the weekend. Field trials have already begun on all four contenders, according to Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara. “The aim is to bring these solutions up to the required level as quickly as possible and scale up production to thousands of units,” he said on Saturday. But devising the technology and deploying it are two very different challenges. “Offensive capabilities always stay one step ahead of defensive ones,” said the deputy head of the President’s Office, Pavlo Palisa, on Friday. “We will certainly have to adapt. This will take time.” One of the Ukrainian-made interceptors that is showing promise, called the Sting, is reported to have brought down two of the jet-powered drones in recent days. Another Ukrainian company, F-Drones, has updated its interceptor. “Russia is now deploying jet-powered Shahed drones, so we built LITAVR+. The upgraded interceptor reaches speeds of over 400 km/h,” it said on X. Countering jet-powered drones is also at the top of the agenda of former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who has begun a visit to the United States to explore areas of cooperation with defense technology companies “and organizations that can become partners in our new projects and help strengthen Ukraine.” “We also plan to build new ventures from scratch around the technologies that are critically needed on the battlefield today,” Fedorov posted on X, including robotics to “remove personnel from the most dangerous front-line sectors,” and low-cost AI-guided missiles. Russian Banderol targets Ukraine’s maritime corridor The battle to win a technological edge in the conflict is never-ending. While Ukraine has successfully expanded its range of mid- and long-range strike drones, Russia has developed a cheap cruise missile it has dubbed the Banderol. The five-meter- (16-foot-) long missile has a maximum speed of 385 to 405 miles per hour (620–650 kilometers an hour) and a reported range of up to 310 miles (500 kilometers). It carries a 330-pound (150-kilogram) warhead. Its range is sufficient to cover much of southern Ukraine when launched from helicopters over Crimea. Dozens of Banderols have been used against the port of Odessa in recent weeks, interrupting Ukraine’s grain exports. Since the beginning of August, Ukraine has exported 1.4 million tons of grain and oilseeds, according to Taras Vysotskyi, minister of agrarian policy – only about one-third of the potential export volume. The Banderol attacks have significantly slowed operations along Ukraine’s maritime corridor through the Black Sea, Ukrainian Navy spokesman Dmytro Pletenchuk said early in August. The constant attacks are making insurance for grain shipments too expensive, according to industry sources. Analysts say the Russian military may be preparing to launch the Banderol from ground-based platforms as well as drones and helicopters. Former Defense Minister Fedorov, who was dismissed by Zelensky in July and is now working in a private capacity, has warned that Ukraine is “gradually, slowly losing” the war. While in Washington, he told the Financial Times that the situation changed month-to-month, but he warned that Russia’s recent air strikes and ever-intensifying use of missiles and advanced drones were critical challenges. “Right now, if we don’t respond to these issues, they will smash us,” he said.

articles.title: Everything We Bought in August 2026 | NBC Selected
articles.summary: This month, our staff bought new products and tested items from brands like Adidas, Béis, Hoka, Apple and more.
articles.body: August starts off deceptively slow for many, but it’s actually a big month of discovery for the shopping experts on our team. The laid-back nature of those first couple of weeks is often welcome following an eventful July. But just before the month comes to an end, everything seems to feel fast-paced again — students are heading back to school, people are squeezing in their last-minute summer vacations and sports fans are prepping for Premier League and football season. At NBC Selected, we’re always in the process of testing some sort of footwear, skin care product or interesting new piece of tech — the types just vary based on the season. This August, everyone on staff tried out a mix of self-bought products and samples (sent complimentary for testing purposes) from some of our favorite brands, which includes Adidas, Shark, Zara, Béis, Phlur and many more. Below, we’re sharing all of the products we tried out this month, including comfortable shoes, hair gel, carry-on luggage, lunch boxes, and tank tops that are so good we bought them (or would buy them) with our own money. The best products we tried in August 2026 All of the products below are either courtesy brand samples or products that we bought ourselves. Zoe Malin, reporter There’s always a couple pairs of shoes that it seems like every woman in Manhattan owns, and this year, one of them is the Adidas Handball Spezial, specifically in the Earth Strata/Off White/Gum color. After weeks of seeing them at least five times a day, I convinced myself I needed them — I even started planning outfits around them in my head, so I had no choice but to buy them. I’ve been wearing them multiple times a week for a month now. The sneakers are just as stylish as I imagined, and even more comfortable than I hoped for. They support my feet as I walk more than 20,000 steps a day in New York City, and the brown shade makes them a neutral basic that pairs well with the majority of my outfits. Two sizing notes: I went down half a size in these because I felt like they ran big when I tried them on at the store (I got a women’s 8 instead of my typical 8.5), and they’re narrow in the toe area, so if you have wide feet, they may not work for you. One of the ingredients I must have in my kitchen is Maldon Sea Salt Flakes. I sprinkle it on everything I eat to bring out the natural flavor of food and add crunch, including eggs, roasted vegetables, baked fish, pasta, ice cream and oatmeal. Whenever I run out, which I did this month, I buy the 20-ounce tub. It has a resealable lid, so it lasts me about six months; I keep it on my counter and grab a big pinch as needed. Not to be dramatic, but the few days between when I ran out of sea salt flakes and when my new tub came were tasteless — it’s that essential to my meals. Curly hair styling is always a common theme in my TikTok algorithm, but I’ve been served even more videos about it lately, which prompted me to reconsider my routine. I consulted my hairdresser at Curl Bar Beauty, who approved of what I saw on social media and gave me more in-depth lessons based on my exact hair type. She recommended I use a foam and a gel instead of a mousse and a cream, the latter of which weighs down my thick hair too much. I also finish with a few spritzes of my beloved Color Wow Dream Coat for Curly Hair. My hairdresser instructed me to apply these products to soaking wet hair, use a cotton T-shirt or paper towels to soak up excess moisture, air dry (or, better yet, diffuse if I have time) and break my curl cast with a little oil. Lover Ur Curls offered to send me their Volumizing Foam and Strong Hold Gel when I was overhauling my hair styling routine. I’ve been testing them for about six weeks and truly feel like my curls have never looked as defined and shiny, or felt as soft. They also maintain their shape much better over about two days between sleeping and workouts. At $22 and $24, the foam and gel are half the price of what I was paying for similar products, so I’m less stingy about how much I use at a time, which has also contributed to my improved curl definition. Now, with a combination of the right products and a styling method I can actually commit to, I’m even more confident about my natural hair. After a super hot, sweaty run, I always crave fruit punch, so I usually drink a Gatorade Zero. But when I was on vacation in Maine this month, the nearby market only had Local Weather’s Fruit Punch Premium Sport Drink — it seemed close enough to Gatorade, so I bought it. It tastes exactly like the Hawaiian Punch I had as a kid but with way less sugar and lots of electrolytes from coconut water and sea salt. As I drank it, I started to feel much less depleted, and the flavor was delicious, so I actually enjoyed sipping it. I looked forward to buying a Local Weather each day after my run during my trip, so I ordered a 12-pack when I got home since I haven’t seen them in Manhattan grocery stores or bodegas yet. I meal prep overnight oats for breakfast during the work week, and nut butter is one of my favorite toppings in addition to berries, coconut flakes and pecans. I usually go with plain almond butter, but Big Spoon Roasters sent me a few of its more unique options, and out of all the ones I tried, I came back to Pistachio Crunch Almond Butter most often. It has just enough maple and sea salt in it that I taste the flavors without them being overpowering, and the pistachios mixed with the almonds adds extra richness. I also love spreading the Pistachio Crunch Almond Butter on rice cakes with sliced bananas before a run. I don’t think I’ll be able to go back to eating standard almond butter once I finish this jar. Caitlin Cusack, associate social media editor I absolutely love when my skin looks shiny, glittery and bronzed, especially in the summer. When I saw that Phlur launched this shimmery body oil, I was beyond excited to try it out. Out of all of the glittery body oils I’ve tested (which is at least 5), I can confidently say that this one is my favorite. The formula is extremely pigmented, so I only need to use a little bit at a time, and it’s actually noticeable to the eye and in pictures. It’s also extremely long lasting — I can put this on in the morning before lunch and get home at night with it looking fresh. My only complaint is that it’s a little sticky right after application — which is not ideal if you’re like me and always get ready super last-minute. Last month, Béis dropped a fully overhauled collection of travel essentials, which included an updated version of the brand’s insanely popular OG weekender bag. We stopped by its New York City popup event to chat with founder Shay Mitchell, and I was lucky enough to take home the revamped weekender bag, which I tested out on my trip to Chicago earlier this month. I used this bag as my personal item on the flight, and was extremely impressed with how much I was able to pack — it fit all of my toiletries, hair tools, a pair of shoes and even my travel-sized Lola Blanket. My favorite part of this bag is the soft opening, which allowed me to stuff my blanket on top of all of my things while still being able to fit the bag underneath the seat in front of me. I used the trolley sleeve to carry the bag on top of my rolling carry-on, and it made my airport experience easy. I’ve been looking for a great coffee tumbler for a while, and after trying a bunch, I realized that all I wanted was to see my coffee. Not sure what the psychology behind that is, but when I found this clear iced coffee tumbler from Nespresso, I knew it was exactly what I wanted. Although it’s technically not insulated, it keeps my iced lattes cold for hours. I can make my coffee with ice at home, bring it to the office and still see ice cubes until at least noon. It’s also *actually* spill resistant. I’ve thrown this in my bag plenty of times and haven’t had an issue with spilling one time. Plus, all of the pieces are dishwasher safe, so it’s super easy to clean. As a years-long Color Wow Dream Coat fan, I was skeptical when e.l.f. launched a similar anti-frizz styling product for more than half the price. But after trying it out on a blowout, I was extremely impressed. My blowout looked shiny, silky and not frizzy at all immediately after styling, and it held up great throughout my humid commute and full day at the office. My only complaint is that the nozzle doesn’t distribute the product that quickly, so it takes a while to cover my entire head. But, I’d take an achy wrist in exchange for a blowout that actually lasts throughout the day. And for just $9? I’m already planning to stock up before this product sells out. I’m a huge fan of Ninja’s OG espresso machine, the Ninja Luxe Cafe. So when the brand dropped their first fully automatic espresso machine, I was excited to try it out. After testing it over the last few weeks, I can confidently say that this machine has fixed all of my pain points that come with the Ninja Luxe Cafe. Since it’s fully automatic, you basically don’t have to do any of the manual work you once did. This machine grinds the beans, tamps your espresso, brews your coffee and discards the grounds, all with the press of a single button. Plus, it does a full machine rinse after every single use, so I have a little peace of mind that the inside of my machine is clean. The biggest pain point is definitely the price — $900 is a lot of money, but I think it’s worth it for a machine that’s basically a personal barista living in your kitchen, especially if you’re a real coffee lover. Marilyn La Jeunesse, newsletter editor I have always been a vanilla girl. The obsession started back in middle school with Victoria’s Secret Vanilla Lace and has been going strong ever since. Lately, I’ve been on the hunt for more mature vanilla scents that feel refined and intriguing. Phlur’s new Vanilla Canyon is just that. The scent reminds me of fall days in Southern California, the notes of wild honey and patchouli are warm and familiar. It wears well throughout the day and feels like the perfect elevated vanilla for every day wear. I’m a carry-on only traveler who can easily survive a two-week vacation living out of a single tiny suitcase. After my old Monos suitcase needed to be retired, I requested Away’s The Bigger Carry-On Flex to test on upcoming trips. I didn’t think the extra two inches of space would make such a difference, but I was instantly impressed when I was able to easily fit two pairs of shoes, five heavy dresses, two pairs of shorts, three shirts, my toiletry bag, and all my undergarments inside with room to spare. This suitcase is an absolute workhorse that glides like a breeze over airport floors and other terrain. The one con is that, both times I boarded my plane, the gate agents flagged the suitcase because its height is very obvious. While I was able to put the bag in the overhead bin, anyone wanting to avoid the dreaded gatecheck may want to opt for the regular size of The Carry-On Flex. As someone with androgenic alopecia and naturally thin hair, I don’t usually put my hair up. Normally, I’m very self-conscious about gaps and don’t feel like investing in claw clips or cute hair ties is really worth my money — until I got a sample of Wet Brush x Hill House’s new collaboration. For the first time in a long time, I actually wanted to wear my hair up, excited to show off all the fun patterns. While I am still insecure about the way my hair looks when it’s tied up, having cute accessories (that are surprisingly affordable) make me feel a bit more confident. Despite being a huge bath person (I take at least one steamy bath a week, even during the summer), I never knew bath tub filters existed until a colleague tested them for work. I tested the Canopy Bath Tub Filter, and was surprised at not only how easy it was to install (it took less than two minutes) and how cute it looks on my spout. There’s also a built-in temperature indicator on the side of the filter that tells you when the water is too hot — a huge bonus for anyone who tends to turn their water on full blast. Shalwah Evans, senior editor Back in May I bought a pair of these sneakers in a different color as a birthday gift to myself. They’re so comfortable that I got them in this neutral cream for that end-of-summer into fall transitional weather. The gum bottom has just the right amount of traction so that when I’m running for the train I don’t worry about slipping. I will wear these well into the winter if the weather permits — they are that stylish and easy. It had been a while since I’d bought anything from Zara, but when I needed a basic tank it’s one of the first stores that came to mind — and it didn’t fail me. I love this top because it’s a neutral color but doesn’t look too simple. I can wear it with so many things in my wardrobe. Additionally, it didn’t have weird straps that were too puny to cover my bra straps (I hate fiddling with them all day) and it was fitted in a way that gave me support during that time of the month when my top is heavy and sensitive. I bring my own coffee everywhere I go because I only drink one type, which means I run through coffee mugs quickly. My Yeti is by far my favorite but it’s large and I wanted something a little smaller and lighter. This kids’ rambler is the perfect size for my one cup of 6-ounce coffee, it has a leakproof top so I don’t have to worry about spills if I need to throw it in my bag during my morning commute, and it’s dishwasher safe so I just drop it in there when I get home. I also love that it has a top handle for carrying, so I can hold onto the bottle and a subway pole with the same hand. I’ll likely never use the straw, but it doesn’t take away from the function of the bottle so I don’t mind it. I’m actually thinking about getting two more so I’ll have a Yeti for each work day. Mili Godio, updates editor We’re huge fans of Grace & Stella eye masks here at NBC Selected, and these brightening patches (which the brand launched last month) are no exception. I slap these under my eyes nearly every morning before work and they make a noticeable difference. I look so much brighter and more awake, and my genetic dark circles look a little less intense. Ashley Morris, associate reporter, seo In the past few years, Meiji Meji has become one of my favorite brands to follow, and I happened to be visiting home during its Toronto pop-up and managed to pick up a few pieces. I’m obsessed with the brand’s aesthetic, which features bold and bright colors inspired by the founder’s Nigerian roots, with stunning, unique graphics as the cornerstone of its design. The Danfo skirt is mini without being too short (not that that’s a problem to me), and fits well. I was worried about choosing the wrong size, but the brand has a sister sizes page that shows women of different sizes in the garments, so you can get a better idea of what may work for you. I also love the fit and soft, stretchy feel of the Ko Mi Je No Rush top, which gets me compliments every time I wear it. I’ve actually had the cycling jersey since the start of the summer, but they go together perfectly. A few months of wear has only further confirmed that I’m 100 percent on board the Meji Meji train — it’s honestly only a matter of time before I make another purchase. When Aest Studios reached out to me to send me a bag to test, I had to do a double take — never would I have imagined such a chic camera bag. It’s made from a soft yet durable washed calf leather, which has a deliciously worn-in look that’s perfect for conveying an effortless vibe. It has magnetic pockets on the side that I love to fill with my cards and lip glosses, along with a removable interior divider that keeps my camera separate from all of my other bag fillings. Camera or not though, I’ve been carrying this bag everywhere: errands, parties, the office, you name it — yes it’s a great camera bag, but in my opinion, it’s an even better everyday bag. I’ve had this top for a short while and it’s already become an essential in my wardrobe. When I initially received it from the brand, the first thing I noticed was the texture. It was soft, yet still had a firm feel to it, and best of all, was completely opaque. A non-sheer white top is hard to come by these days, and that immediately got me excited to wear it. Since then, I’ve worn it at least twice a week, and it’s been the ideal summer top. It’s not too heavy, versatile enough to pair with just about any bottom in my wardrobe, and easy to wash and get right back to wearing (with no yellow armpits yet). Bethany Heitman, commerce editor My 5-year-old daughter is going into kindergarten and I’ve been focused on getting her ready with all the necessary supplies. We tested backpacks and State Bags were far and away our favorite. So, of course, I needed to buy her the matching lunchbox. articles.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker equates Israel's 'right to exist' to Nazi Germany
articles.summary: Hasan Piker compared Israel's right to exist to Nazi Germany and called Zionism a fascist ideology during his appearance on "The Breakfast Club."
articles.body: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker equated Israel's "right to exist" to Nazi Germany on Saturday during an interview on "The Breakfast Club," calling it an "apartheid state." "I think Israel in its current formation, given that it’s a settler colonial operation that’s seeking out the expulsion or complete extermination of the indigenous population as an apartheid state does not have a right to exist," he said. "It’s like, for me, it’s like saying does Nazi Germany have a right to exist or does apartheid South Africa have a right to exist? Does Rhodesia have a right to exist? No, of course not." Host of "The Breakfast Club," Charlamagne tha God, asked if it was like saying MAGA didn't have a right to exist, and Piker said yes. "That doesn't mean kill all Republicans or whatever, right? I mean, I'm sure that's how people would present it as. I mean, this is a trick that every political movement deploys, right?" Piker responded. HASAN PIKER CLAIMS ISRAEL HAS NO ‘RIGHT TO EXIST’ IN ITS CURRENT FORM WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS He added, "So the, 'Does Israel have a right to exist?' deployment as a statement, as a question, is a technique to shift the conversation away from Israel's crimes against the Palestinians to make it seem like the opposition is actually being crazy, and they want like all Jews to be exterminated, all Israelis to be exterminated, which is not the case. That's not a real point of advocacy, it's certainly not my advocacy," the streamer continued. UCLA professor Benjamin Radd refuted Piker's characterization of Israel in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Piker’s comments about Israel as a ‘settler colonial operation’ and its alleged objective of ‘seeking out the expulsion or complete extermination’ of one of the region’s indigenous groups reflects a profound ignorance of the historical development of the land, and of the various ethnic, religious, and colonial-imperial powers — including the Ottoman Turks — that have traded control over it. If Piker were intellectually honest, he could hold two uncomfortable truths simultaneously: that different groups, including Jews, have legitimate indigenous claims and that the current Israeli leadership does not represent nor serve as an indictment of those claims," Radd said. Piker, an outspoken anti-Israel voice, also compared Zionism to fascism and Nazi Germany during the conversation. "I think the reason why the Israeli society broadly has shifted so far to the right in a matter of decades is because of this ideology that guides Israeli society. It’s Zionism, which I, by the way, have no problems like, equating to fascism because it is a fascist ideology and even make these comparisons to Nazi Germany, which is very frustrating for a lot of people. They say that’s antisemitic," he said. Piker has divided the Democratic Party, as some have chosen to embrace the streamer and others have denounced him. HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has campaigned with Piker and has dismissed any focus on his controversial statements. Though, recently, El-Sayed has put some distance between himself and the streamer. El-Sayed, who is facing off against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in battleground Michigan in a high-stakes Senate showdown, on Monday emphasized in a statement, "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople." The statement from El-Sayed came after Piker, on his stream last week, featured an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel. articles.title: Over 6,000 Ebola cases confirmed in DRC as death toll nears 3,000
articles.summary: Outbreak in the DRC ‘the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded,’ as country struggles to contain infections.
articles.body:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has topped prior surges – becoming the worst the country has experienced – as new data confirms there are now over 6,000 confirmed cases and nearly 3,000 deaths.

There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which is rapidly spreading across the country.

The current Ebola outbreak is “the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded”, according to United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as people continue to be infected with the virus faster than frontline workers can track and respond to new cases. This is partly due to many new infections occurring among people who are not being monitored through contract tracing, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

The DRC Ministry of Communications said on social media that 6,041 cases have been confirmed, “including 1,366 recoveries and 2,911 deaths. [Another] 619 patients are in isolation or hospitalised.”

The response to the outbreak faces several challenges as cases are mostly concentrated in the eastern provinces of the DRC where densely-populated areas experience insecurity related to armed conflict, displacement and pre-existing humanitarian challenges.

The medical charity Doctors Without Borders says existing health needs, as well as airport closures and flight restrictions, are complicating the provision of healthcare, disrupting the flow of staff, diagnostics, referrals and supply chains.

Frontline healthcare workers went on strike in early August to protest their unpaid wages and the dire working conditions.

Uganda was declared free of the Ebola virus after no new cases were reported for 42 days on August 28.

articles.title: Company offering reward for safe return of truckload of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer
articles.summary: Police say a thief presented false documentation at a California distribution centre before driving off with the shipment.
articles.body:
Pabst Brewing Company has turned to social media for help locating thousands of cans of its Blue Ribbon beer taken from a distribution centre in California.

"STOLEN," the company announced. "To the thief: we don't fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honourable way."

The alleged thief presented false documentation at an Anheuser-Busch distribution centre in Montclair, police said, and made off with a shipment worth $25,000 (£18,500) that had been destined for San Diego.

Pabst says it is being "deadly serious" about the "ridiculous" incident and is offering a reward for help finding the 40,000lbs (18,144kg) of beer.

It was the second theft on the same day from the same distribution centre, Montclair Police said in a statement. Police are investigating whether "they were committed as part of the same fraudulent cargo-theft operation".

In the first incident, a shipment worth $45,000 (£33,000) headed for Tucson, Arizona, was picked up on 17 August but had not arrived at its destination two weeks on.

An hour later, police say thieves used fraudulent documents to pick up the Pabst Blue Ribbon beer.

"Investigators identified similarities between the two incidents," police said. "Information provided regarding the trucking company, driver and vehicles involved contained discrepancies and is currently being investigated."

Although they are separate companies, Anheuser-Busch has a contract to brew Pabst Blue Ribbon beer. It is unclear if the Arizona-bound shipment also contained PBR beer.

"What we discovered was it was just a bad actor essentially who came in and pretended to be the person who was supposed to pick up the beer," a spokesperson told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

"It wasn't the person who was supposed to pick up the beer and then they drove off with it."

The company sought to underscore the seriousness of the crime in its social media post.

"We realise how ridiculous that sounds, but it's the truth," it said. "This is real and we are deadly serious."

Pabst also had a message for the thief: "Pabst is officially starting the clock now - you have exactly 18 days and 44 minutes to return our truckload of beer, no questions asked." The number is a nod to the company's year of founding: 1844.

The company is also offering an unspecified reward for the return of the shipment.

articles.title: Photos: Nearly 1,000 dead, thousands missing in Nepal–China border floods
articles.summary: Over 4,000 people remain missing after deadly floods swept through Nepal and Tibet, leaving families in despair.
articles.body:
Devastating floods near Nepal’s border with China have killed at least 939 people, the country’s disaster authority says, as the death toll continues to rise and rescue efforts enter a sixth day.

Chinese state media has confirmed a further 16 deaths in Tibet, bringing the known regional toll to 955, with 4,471 people still missing on both sides of the border.

Nepal’s latest figures list 3,925 people missing nationwide, including 592 foreigners. Many of the missing are workers from hydropower projects that took the full force of the torrent, although officials say the number of unaccounted-for hydropower staff fell to 639 on Monday from an earlier count of 933.

The disaster agency says 3,333 Nepali citizens remain missing, with some of the worst-hit areas including Nuwakot district, where 1,158 people are unaccounted for, and neighbouring Rasuwa, with 865 missing. The missing also includes 45 army soldiers, 38 police officers and 18 customs and immigration officials.

In neighbouring India, authorities in Uttar Pradesh state say they have recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims, though they are not yet included in the official toll.

articles.title: 'Justice and hope': Campaigners hail UK PM Andy Burnham's vow to end indefinite jail terms
articles.summary: UK News: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to end the controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, saying people will no longer r.
articles.body: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to end the controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, saying people will no longer remain trapped indefinitely under a punishment abolished more than a decade ago, The Guardian reported.Burnham announced on Sunday that legislation would be brought in by the end of the current parliament to terminate the open-ended sentences.The move was welcomed by campaigners who have spent years pushing for reforms and called it a long-awaited step towards justice for thousands of affected families.“This will finally bring justice and hope to IPPs and their families," Bernadette Emerson, co-founder of the IPP Solidarity Movement, was quoted as saying by The Independent.IPP sentences were introduced in 2005 for offenders considered a continuing risk to the public. Prisoners were given a minimum tariff but no fixed maximum term, meaning they could remain behind bars even after completing the minimum period. Although the system was abolished in 2012, the decision was not retrospective.As of June 30, 856 people were still in prison under IPP sentences, according to figures from the Ministry of Justice and HM Prison and Probation Service.Eight in 10 of those prisoners had spent at least 10 years in jail beyond the minimum term at which they could have applied for parole. Another 1,415 people who had been released under IPP sentences had been recalled to custody.Campaigners welcomed Burnham's announcement but called for swift implementation and support for prisoners transitioning out of custody and off IPP licences.Marc Conway, CEO of campaign group United Group for Reform of IPP (UNGRIPP), said the announcement marked an important step after years of campaigning.Conway, himself a former IPP prisoner, said legislation alone could not undo the damage caused by the system but was necessary to begin addressing it.The IPP regime has also been linked to severe mental health struggles among prisoners and their families. Tommy Nicol, who received a four-year minimum tariff for robbery, died by suicide in 2015 after spending years in prison.His sister Donna has campaigned for an end to the system, saying the government's pledge came too late for her brother.Burnham said the government would take a "very careful" approach to ending the sentences, particularly because some prisoners could still pose a risk to the public.He also announced plans for a cross-party oversight group to examine how the changes would be implemented."There are still individuals who will pose a risk to communities," Burnham said, stressing that public safety and national security would be considered while bringing the system to an end.According to The Independent, almost 2,300 people remain affected by IPP sentences, including more than 800 who have never been released.The government is expected to bring forward legislation before the end of the parliamentary term, with further details on how individual cases will be handled to be worked out under the proposed oversight process.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino told Fox News Digital Monday that the reversal had not resolved her concerns. articles.title: Palestinian farmers rebuild what Israeli settlers destroy in West Bank
articles.summary: Israeli settler pogroms destroy greenhouses and crops, but Burin’s farmers insist on rebuilding.
articles.body:
Burin, occupied West Bank – Ghassan Najjar’s phone starts ringing the moment the Israeli army rolls into Burin. It happens most days now – the whirring convoy of armoured personnel carriers working its way through the village’s narrow streets as soldiers fan out to shutter shops one by one.

Along with roughly two dozen other farmers, Najjar is a member of Burin’s Land and Farming Cooperative. They know that they don’t have the capability to fight back against Israel’s military might with arms so instead focus on the land and keeping their connection to it.

But in addition to the military raids, they also face settler attacks, part of a pogrom against Palestinians that has reached fever pitch across the West Bank. Those settlers live in outposts and settlements built on occupied Palestinian land, which makes them illegal under international law.

On July 13, a settler tried to graze his flock inside one of the cooperative’s five greenhouses. Cooperative members struggled to keep the livestock away until Israeli border police arrived. Najjar recalled challenging the officers over why a settler had been permitted onto land the army itself had designated a closed military zone, from which Israeli citizens are, on paper, also barred.

The settler left angry. In Arabic, he told Najjar: “You’ll see.”

The next night, roughly 10 settlers arrived, gutting all five of the cooperative’s greenhouses, cutting away their plastic sheeting and destroying their irrigation networks.

The damage, by the cooperative’s estimate, ran to roughly 30,000 shekels (about $10,000) in plastic sheeting alone. About 9,000 tomato seedlings worth 8,000 shekels ($2,670) had been bought that same morning for planting. They died within hours because there was nowhere else to put them.

For a cooperative that pools land, labour and produce among about 25 families, the loss reverberated beyond the five greenhouses themselves. “We’re talking about 25 families working inside the cooperative,” Najjar said. “This year is the most difficult year for the cooperative. We’re facing many attacks by the settlers and the army.”

Just weeks later, Burin lost more than 1,500 olive and other trees, according to Najjar. Some were burned by settlers. Others were cut down or uprooted by military bulldozers along a local route accessible to Israelis but not Palestinians.

The wheat harvest fared little better: Of the 10,000sq metres (2.5 acres) the cooperative planted, 7,000sq metres (1.7 acres) were burned before farmers could harvest the crop this summer. These days, most of Burin’s farmland sits in closed military zones – renewed, Najjar said, every month or two. On paper, such orders are issued on security grounds to keep out attacking settlers ; in practice, they apply overwhelmingly to the Palestinian landowners the settlers are attacking.

The pattern extends far beyond Burin. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded 1,418 settler attacks this year resulting in casualties or property damage across the West Bank through July, a rate that is on pace to eclipse 2025’s record high of 1,836 such attacks. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and other human rights organisations have accused Israeli authorities of enabling settler attacks and described their cumulative effect on Palestinian communities as contributing to forced displacement.

It is in this context that Najjar and the cooperative’s members have developed what they call the “Tom and Jerry Programme” after the cartoon.

“We go to the land early every morning,” he explained. “When the army comes, we run away. And when the army goes, we come back again.”

“Even if we don’t have planting or harvesting to do on the land, we [go to] drink coffee – to tell the settlers and the army that this is our land and we’re not going to leave it,” he said.

Najjar founded the Land and Farming Cooperative in March 2020, weeks before COVID-19 lockdowns reached the West Bank. It started with five members and now counts about 25, 17 of them women, who farm roughly 25,000sq metres (6 acres) around Burin together.

The idea, he said, was never simply agricultural. “We’re not just a cooperative that plants vegetables and sells them,” Najjar said. “For us, the cooperative straddles the economic and the political because everything is connected.”

He described the cooperative as fighting on three fronts at once: the Israeli occupation, what he calls the “bureaucracy” of the Palestinian Authority and the “umbrella” of capitalism and the NGO funding structures that come, in his telling, with strings attached.

Fifteen percent of everything the cooperative sells goes back into the village, funding children’s and women’s programming. Twenty families it considers most in need once received free vegetables outright. The cooperative has since shifted towards helping those families cultivate small plots of their own under what members call their “don’t give me fish; teach me to fish” programme.

“This is the real food sovereignty,” Najjar said. “People who don’t eat from what they’ve grown will never have real freedom.”

Before joining, new members undergo six months of training covering both the political economy of the occupation and the practicalities of agroecology, including how to treat soil and pest problems without resorting to chemicals. Every two weeks, the cooperative meets to plan their work. At the end of each month, members evaluate what succeeded.

Much of the vision for the cooperative, Najjar said, was drafted while he attended what he calls “the Palestinian school of revolution”: Israeli prison. Two months after the cooperative was founded, Najjar was placed under administrative detention, under which Israeli authorities hold Palestinians without charge or trial and detention orders may be renewable indefinitely. Najjar spent roughly a year in prison, four months of it in isolation.

“In isolation, I thought a lot about the cooperative because, to be honest, it gives you the time to think,” he said. “I wrote all the procedures and the goals for the cooperative – exactly what we needed.” By the time he was released, cooperative members had built two additional greenhouses and brought three more plots of land under cultivation in his absence.

“The cooperative is not for us,” he said. “If Ghassan gets arrested, if Ghassan dies, if Ghassan is travelling, the cooperative doesn’t close. It’s for the farmers, for Burin, for whoever believes in freedom and food sovereignty.”

By Najjar’s count, the July attack was the seventh time the cooperative has had its greenhouses vandalised or destroyed. Asked what drives members to keep rebuilding structures that may simply be torn down again, he returns, over and over, to dignity.

“This is the work between the evil and the right. You have to decide which side you’re going to be on,” he said. “We decided to be at the front of the struggle because this is our land. We connect our dignity to the land, and I don’t think anyone in this world can live without dignity.”

As closed military zones have become the norm, Burin – sandwiched between the notoriously violent settlements of Yitzhar and Har Brakha and the Givat Ronen outpost – has seen 13 outposts established or expanded in recent months, by Najjar’s count. But as people in the village have shifted from regarding his politics with bemusement to respect, Najjar sees the cooperative’s persistence as proof of a more fundamental victory.

“The real occupation is not when they create the checkpoint and invade the village,” he said. “The real occupation is if they occupy your mind. When you are waking up in the morning and working your land – this is the real freedom.”

For now, that resolve manifests in early morning “Tom and Jerry” trips to their lands and in replacing what was destroyed alongside building a fence organisers hope will at least slow the next attack.

“We prefer to die on our land rather than accept another Nakba,” Najjar said. “We work as a family, we work as comrades and we work for freedom.

“We’re not working just for economic reasons or for ‘peace’,” he added. “F*** ‘peace’. I care about freedom. And when you work the land, you feel you have freedom, even if you are under attack by the settler.”

articles.title: US Fish and Wildlife Service officer dies during wildfire evacuation efforts in Oklahoma, agency says
articles.summary: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service officer David Taylor was going door-to-door to evacuate Oklahoma families when he made his last contact with dispatch.
articles.body: A federal wildlife officer is believed to have died while helping evacuate residents threatened by a wildfire in Oklahoma, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said over the weekend. Officials said David Taylor, 38, of Scio, Oregon, was helping people fleeing the fast-moving fire south of Oklahoma City on Saturday. He was going door-to-door to help residents alongside emergency crews. His last contact with dispatch came while he was assisting a family in leaving their home, the agency said. 11 NATIONAL PARK SERVICE WORKERS EVACUATED BY HELICOPTER AMID CALIFORNIA FIRE "Everything we know about David's actions demonstrates extraordinary courage and selflessness," said U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik. " When people were in danger, David was there helping them get to safety. He remained committed to protecting others under the most dangerous circumstances. We mourn alongside his family, friends and colleagues, and we will never forget his service." Evidence recovered from a structure led officials to believe Taylor died during the evacuation effort, authorities said. MARINE VETERAN AND BOSTON FIREFIGHTER DIES AFTER RESCUE EFFORTS AT MASSIVE HOUSE BLAZE At the time of his death, Taylor was a senior chief petty officer in the Navy Reserve and previously served on active duty. During his 20 years of naval service, Taylor completed five deployments, including one to Iraq and four to Djibouti. Taylor also served the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service at the Rio Mora National Wildlife Refuge and the Las Vegas National Wildlife Refuge in New Mexico before joining the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge in Oklahoma. The Fish and Wildlife Service and the Department of the Interior were coordinating support for Taylor’s family and co-workers, the agency said. articles.title: Spanish prime minister points finger at Israel, Russia disinformation over Ceuta migrant crisis
articles.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation about Spain’s approach to migration, fueling this summer’s migrant crisis at the border of Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. “After July 30 and 31, rumors and disinformation spread on social networks linked to Russia and Israel, and to an…
articles.body:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation about Spain’s approach to migration, fueling this summer’s migrant crisis at the border of Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

“After July 30 and 31, rumors and disinformation spread on social networks linked to Russia and Israel, and to an ultra-right international that always uses migration to attack both Spain and Europe and divide it,” Sánchez told Cadena Ser radio, Al Jazeera reported .

The prime minister cited research from the European Union’s European External Action Service as indicating that Israeli and Russian platforms have spread disinformation in collaboration with far-right networks, according to Reuters.

Sánchez said it was “evident” that both countries used the large, unprecedented influx of migrants to criticize his government in response to Madrid’s stances “regarding the genocide in Gaza or [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.”

More than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta late last month at one of the few land borders shared between the EU and Africa, Reuters reported. Local authorities said that at least 100 people died in the aftermath.

Sánchez emphasized that the crisis in Ceuta “can only be resolved through cooperation and not through distrust towards Morocco.” He pledged to provide Ceuta with 168 million euros, or $195 million, in aid.

Israeli Foreign ‌Minister Gideon ⁠Sa’ar slammed Sánchez’s claim, accusing him of “lying shamelessly” on social media .

“This is a brazen lie,” Sa’ar continued. “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin rejects the notion that Russia was involved in the crisis.

“No. Nothing to do with it,” Peskov said, according to Spanish outlet RTVE Noticias .

Spain’s Supreme Court has ruled that migrants stopped at sea as they attempted to reach Ceuta — or Melilla, another Spanish territory — cannot be sent back to Morocco. Spanish officials said 48,000 migrants have voluntarily returned to Morocco.

President Trump and Stephen Miller, the White House’s deputy chief of staff for policy, used the crisis to claim that the same thing could happen in the U.S.

“It’s terrible,” Trump told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich in July. “Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in. If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life.”

articles.title: Water restrictions imposed throughout Israel amid nationwide supply disruption
articles.summary: The warning came amid an unusual disruption to Israel’s national water network, after five of the country’s six desalination facilities shut down. The impact...
articles.body:
The warning came amid an unusual disruption to Israel's national water network, after five of the country's six desalination facilities shut down.

The impact of a widespread malfunction at Israel's desalination facilities reached central Israel on Monday, with residents of Givatayim warned that water supply disruptions could occur in the coming hours, including reduced water pressure and even outages in certain areas.

A message sent to residents stated: "Following problems with the water supply in the national water network, disruptions to water supply may occur in the coming hours, including reduced pressure and water outages in certain areas. We ask the public to conserve water as much as possible and use water only for essential needs until normal operations resume."

The warning came amid an unusual disruption to Israel's national water network, after five of the country's six desalination facilities were forced to shut down. According to Water Authority Director-General Yehezkel Lifshitz, severe seawater turbidity that began over the weekend and moved from south to north has prevented the facilities from filtering water and operating normally.

Five of six desalination facilities shut down

The Water Authority estimates that the turbidity is linked to stormy conditions in the eastern Mediterranean. An initial assessment also suggests that it may have been caused by a significant algae buildup drifting from the Nile region.

A dedicated vessel was sent offshore to collect samples and examine the composition of the material causing the turbidity.

The effects of the malfunction were initially felt mainly in southern Israel and in the agricultural sector. Farmers in the Eshkol Regional Council were asked to immediately reduce their use of freshwater for agriculture and gardening, while the Ramat Negev Regional Council decided to temporarily halt agricultural water supplies and reduce irrigation in gardens and public areas.

Meanwhile, Mekorot was instructed to increase the use of available production and drilling resources across the national water network in order to reduce the shortage created by the desalination shutdown.

The Water Authority estimated that some of the facilities may return to operation in the coming hours as the sediment settles and seawater clarity improves.

Gezer Regional Council imposes water restrictions

The Gezer Regional Council instructed residents to immediately halt watering private gardens and agricultural areas on Monday after failures at Israel's desalination facilities caused a nationwide disruption to the regular water supply.

In a notice issued at 3:50 p.m. on Monday, the council stated: "Due to a nationwide disruption in the regular water supply, as a result of malfunctions at the national desalination facilities, residents of the council are asked to immediately close the taps and water systems designated for home gardens and agriculture."

Water associations were instructed to stop irrigating agricultural areas and public spaces to ensure enough water remained available for private use.

"Reducing water use for gardening and agricultural needs is necessary in order to maintain continuity of household water supplies," the notice said.

At the time of the announcement, the council said that the only community within its jurisdiction experiencing a water outage was Karmi Yosef, but warned that additional communities could be affected by the disruption.

"We ask all residents to act responsibly and conserve water as much as possible," the council said.

The council added that it would provide further updates as needed.

Jerusalem, Rishon Lezion warned of possible water disruptions

Residents of Jerusalem and Rishon Lezion were also warned of possible water supply disruptions on Monday after malfunctions at Israel's desalination facilities affected the national water network.

The Hagihon water company, which serves Jerusalem, said that disruptions to desalination facility operations could lead to water outages and interruptions in the capital.

"We are working with the relevant authorities to reduce disruptions and restore regular water supply as soon as possible," the company said in a message to customers.

Hagihon said customers affected by the malfunction would receive individual notifications and added that there was no need to stockpile water at this stage.

"If supply disruptions occur in your area, we will update you regarding the locations of water distribution points and their operating hours," the company said.

The company also urged residents to follow updates on its website and through its customer service center.

Meanwhile, residents of Rishon Lezion were warned of possible disruptions following a nationwide water supply issue involving Mekorot, Israel's national water company, and in accordance with Water Authority instructions.

The Maniv Rishon water corporation said that Mekorot and the Water Authority had issued a nationwide request for residents to conserve water and avoid nonessential uses, including filling pools, washing reservoirs and watering gardens.

Maniv Rishon said it was prepared for such situations and had been working since the morning to maintain a continuous water supply as much as possible, in coordination with the Rishon Lezion Municipality, the Water Authority and Mekorot.
