articles.title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's estate says DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, just as she wanted.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville.

The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later.

Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said.

"DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said.

DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer.

She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said.

DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial.

"It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said.

"This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan."

Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon , philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media.

"A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said.

articles.title: Heaton Park synagogue attack memorial service attended by 800
articles.summary: The Chief Rabbi and Angela Rayner are among those at the event, nearly a year on from the attack.
articles.body:
The Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner are among about 800 people attending a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.

Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.

A service of remembrance began at the synagogue in Manchester at 20:00 BST, with relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors among the speakers.

Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.

He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation – and British Jews more widely – feeling increasingly vulnerable.

Two seats remain empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.

In a message read out at the start of the service, King Charles said: "My wife and I hold all those whose lives were so tragically disrupted by that terrible day most closely in our thoughts and prayers.

"Though the months have passed, the sense of shock and sorrow remains undiminished.

"The memory of those who lost their lives, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, and of those who were injured, Andrew Franks, Bernard Agyemang and Yoni Finlay, remain especially vivid in my mind."

He concluded: "Hatred can never prevail over our shared humanity."

Raphi Bloom, chair of the Yom Kippur Commemoration, said the service was "not only about remembrance" but was also about resilience and "honouring Melvin and Adrian by ensuring that Jewish life continues to flourish".

He said "the wounds remain, but so does our spirit" and, together, they were sending a simple message that they would not be intimidated, defined by hatred or "driven from the place we have called home for more than two centuries".

"As Jews we will stand tall, united, proud and strong," he said.

Referencing Heaton Park and other "sickening terrorist attacks" across the world, Angela Rayner said: "These acts are a crisis for us all - they reflect the increase we've seen in obsessive, intense hatred of Jews."

She said "any attack on Jews is an attack on all of us".

"Together we can overcome and defeat antisemitism – and we will never rest, until every Jewish person is safe."

She said this was "a hatred we must stand robustly against, and root out from its very foundations", which meant "taking on extremists and bearing down on those who seek to divide our communities".

"The only way we can root out this poison is through a whole of society approach."

Yoni Finlay, who was hit by a stray police bullet while helping to barricade the doors during the attack, will also speak at the service.

Earlier, asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about how the Jewish community in the UK feels almost a year on, he said: "I don't think things feel safer, I think we certainly live behind ever increasing gates, more security than we've ever had.

"Jewish people are having to hide their identity. Even my own son, who's in college at the moment, has faced death threats."

Other speakers at the memorial service include Alan Levy, who helped barricade the doors against the attacker, and Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson.

Although the first anniversary of the Heaton Park attack is not until October, the Jewish community will mark it on the religious anniversary rather than by the secular calendar.

The attack happened on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, which falls in September this year.

Rabbi Walker said the service was being held because the community also wanted to hold a public memorial before the Jewish High Holy Days, both to ensure those affected are remembered by wider society and to call for change in society.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul calls for addressing migration causes in Africa
articles.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called for greater efforts to address the causes of the migration crisis in African countries during a visit to Tunis...
articles.body:
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called for greater efforts to address the causes of the migration crisis in African countries during a visit to Tunisia and Algeria.

After meeting with Tunisian Foreign Minister Mohamed Nafti in Tunis on Monday, Wadephul said: "The unstable situation in the Sahel repeatedly contributes to people setting off toward the north, toward Europe."

"We have to tackle the causes together and make sure that the economic situation in these countries genuinely improves," he added.

Wadephul blamed "irresponsible human-smuggling gangs" for the deaths of migrants while travelling through Tunisia, Algeria, Libya and other countries.

Nafti said that many migrants were victims of smuggling networks and were being exploited by criminal gangs. "We should all work together to find solutions to this problem," he said, describing migration as an "important and dangerous issue."

In Tunis, Wadephul was received by President Kais Saied, in an unusual diplomatic gesture for a foreign minister. The minister had previously met representatives of German companies in Tunisia. At a digital centre, he also met representatives of several start-ups.

There, he spoke to a young Tunisian woman who has received a scholarship to study in Germany after achieving the country's best high-school graduation results this year.

Yasmine Yaakoubi, 18, plans to first learn German in Heidelberg and then study engineering in Munich. She said she intends to return to her home country later to use her skills there and give something back to Tunisia.

Wadephul said the two countries could offer each other a great deal, particularly in the field of energy cooperation, in order to jointly create greater growth and prosperity.

"Together, we can turn the Mediterranean into a region of strength between our two continents," he said.

Tunisia and Germany are celebrating the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations this year. According to Wadephul, Germany is Tunisia's third-most important export market.

He said that resilient supply chains were particularly important to the German automotive industry, noting that around 7,500 young Tunisians were studying in Germany, while Tunisian skilled workers made a valuable contribution to Germany's healthcare system.

In the early evening, Wadephul arrived in Algeria, the second stop on his North African tour, where he met Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf.

On Tuesday, the German minister is also due to meet President Abdelmadjid Tebboune. A meeting with representatives of German companies operating in Algeria is also planned.

According to Wadephul, Algeria is already one of the EU's most important gas suppliers.

Its importance is expected to grow further given the country's considerable potential as a future producer and supplier of green hydrogen, the minister said at the start of his trip.

Germany and Algeria agreed in July to significantly deepen their energy supply partnership.

articles.title: Top US general says no plans to send troops to polls for November elections
articles.summary: Remarks come in response to concerns from Democrats that military could be used to interfere in elections.
articles.body:
The chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, the country’s highest ranking military officer, has assured an opposition lawmaker that there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during elections on November 3.

“The Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections,” General Dan Caine said in the letter obtained on Monday by The Associated Press news agency. “Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”

Caine’s letter was addressed to Democratic US Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who recently asked Caine and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to confirm they won’t send troops to the polls. Caine, who advises Hegseth and President Donald Trump on military matters, also wrote: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.”

Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. He said they were needed for immigration enforcement and due to crime and protests.

Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump has been laying the groundwork to claim November’s elections will have been stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 to President Joe Biden and has deployed the National Guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty Marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025.

Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would likely be the National Guard under state control.

“The nonpartisan tradition of military service and the constitutional guardrails that prevent our military from becoming a domestic police force for one political party are essential to maintaining our democracy,” Slotkin said in a news release this month announcing her letters to US military officials. “Thus, our nation’s senior-most defense and security leaders are the final failsafe for our democracy.”

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms.

Sonja Thrasher, Slotkin’s press secretary, said Hegseth has not replied to the letter asking him to confirm troops won’t be deployed to the polls in November.

Slotkin had asked for a response by last Thursday.

In 2020, General Mark Milley, then-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, then a member of the US House of Representatives.

“I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

articles.summary: US News: Anushk Sharma who coaches students for studying abroad made a video appealing to Indian students not to come to the US in the present scenario. It was.
articles.body: Anushk Sharma who coaches students for studying abroad made a video appealing to Indian students not to come to the US in the present scenario. It was not only a warning, but Sharma said it's his earnest request that Indian students should not invest their money to come to the US and then face uncertainty. "I am urging you with folded hands, please don't come to the US now. It's dead," Sharma said in his video that went viral as Indians in the US are facing tough times.The Donald Trump administration has been targeting the H-1B visa program for a long time. But now Indian students are also in lurch as students' visa will only have a 4-year validity and after 4 years, those who need an extension will have to apply. Apart from making it tougher for H-1Bs -- with imposing fees, removing the 60-day grace period after layoff -- the administration is also cracking down on CPT and OPT.Sharma's video was mainly on the recent instructions from the administration to colleges on CPT (Curricular Practical Training) which used to be a temporary work permission for international students. It has nothing to do with immigration authorities, and school authorities can allow a student's job related to the course. In the recent order, the administration said CPT can't be optional; if it's integral to the course, then every student will get this temporary employment, not only international students. And if this does not happen, then the CPT will not be considered necessary for the course.Sharma said CPT is like an internship, and without it, it's almost impossible to get a job in the US. "It's not worth it anymore. I am feeling sad as I am making this video because I used to recommend students to come and study in the US. But now I can't recommend the US. Especially, if you want to study finance, you can go to France, Paris, Oxford, or Cambridge. If you are in tech, go to Germany or Switzerland. You won't get as much salary as in the US, but at least they won't drive you out. If the situation improves in two years, then the US will be the best, but now there is no point in coming. articles.title: Stephen A Smith reveals Barack Obama privately called him after Biden criticism ahead of 2024 election
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith revealed Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his impact, but would not appear on his podcast publicly.
articles.body: Podcast host Stephen A. Smith revealed on Friday that former President Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his influence, noting that Obama wanted to speak privately rather than appear on his podcast. "What I never told y'all, and I never brought up, is that Barack Obama called me too. The content of that conversation will remain private because I will not violate trust," Smith said. "He called before the election to discuss my impact, but he didn't come on the podcast either." Smith spoke to "The Culture Table," hosted by Tori Cooper, Sumatra Abernathy and Ashley Christopher, about receiving a "thumbs-down" award from the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ) at an Atlanta gala, defending himself against the criticism. STEPHEN A SMITH CALLS OUT JILL BIDEN, DEMS FOR 'LYING THROUGH THEIR TEETH' AND DAMAGING PARTY'S BRAND "It was after I said that we need a new president because Joe Biden clearly was done. You know, he clearly looked done. So the point is, folks like to talk to me privately, but then when I ask them to come on camera and to have a fruitful discussion, now they go elsewhere," he continued. "So it's like I'm taking these hits, and these are people that want to facilitate or assist in the facilitation of these narratives being disseminated and projected about me. But the same people calling me privately, having discussions upon which I have never violated. This is the first time anyone has ever heard me publicly state that Barack Obama called me," Smith said. OBAMA BLAMES SPLINTERED MEDIA FOR PREVENTING SUPERSTAR DEMOCRAT FROM RISING UP The former president's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Obama wasn't the only one Smith accused of not coming on his show. He also named former first lady Michelle Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. "I think the Democrats fear my footsteps," he said. "I think they know that they have a legitimate fear that I can influence the election potentially. I will never divulge what was said, but last week when I did my podcast and I responded to the NABJ, I pointed out how Kamala Harris reached out to me and asked to meet with me, and we met for two hours." KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN "She did not speak to me and come on my show before the election," Smith said of Harris. "Once again, in my opinion, they take paths of smaller resistance." Harris' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND Smith recently addressed the NABJ's thumbs-down award during his show. "The reality is that it was a personal hit job," Smith said. "We can sit up there and lollygag around and act like we don't know any better. It was a personal hit job. Which, by the way, usually doesn't phase me. I know you think something phases me, just because you see me commenting on it. No, I'm in this business. I have a platform. I can comment about anything I want to, and I will continue to do so." "That's not what this is," he added. "This is different. This is a journalism organization that didn't engage in journalism when it came to critiquing me. Disparaging Black women is a very incendiary thing to say. If you felt that adamant about it, [NABJ] President [Errin] Haines, how come I never got a call?" Smith speculated that the award was focused on his past criticism of high-profile Black female political figures like Crockett. He also revealed that he reached out to Haines regarding the organization's allegations to potentially discuss their differences, a conversation that ultimately went nowhere. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "While much of the public conversation in recent days has centered on Stephen A. Smith, he was one of five recipients named this year," the NABJ previously told Fox News Digital in a statement. "The concerns NABJ raised extend well beyond any one individual and include threats to editorial independence, the loss of newsroom diversity and reporting expertise, the treatment of Black journalists in the workplace, responsible use of influential media platforms, and decisions that affect the ability of journalists to fully and fairly cover Black communities and hold powerful institutions accountable." Media analyst and Fox News contributor Joe Concha told Fox News Digital that high-profile Democratic figures have rarely appeared on less traditional media platforms, unlike President Donald Trump, who appeared on Joe Rogan's podcast. "Bill Maher has shared the same sentiment: High-profile Democrats want nothing to do with his program, much as they avoid Stephen A. Smith's. The same applies to potential 2028 presidential contenders such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who rarely leaves her political comfort zone, and Kamala Harris, who avoided holding a traditional press conference during her vice presidency and her presidential campaigns because she prefers to control the narrative. "This is the essence of being risk-averse. It is also a losing proposition. Donald Trump joined Joe Rogan for a three-hour interview in 2024 and appeared on other programs, such as Theo Von's, to reach younger male and nonpropensity voters. Harris wanted nothing to do with either. "Similar behavior is evident in Ocasio-Cortez, who struggles when faced with uncomfortable questions, as seen during her appearance in Munich. Conversely, potential 2028 nominees such as JD Vance and Marco Rubio have proven they will take questions from anyone at any time. Ultimately, that kind of exposure can make the difference in a close race." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Lindsay Kornick contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir storms Al-Aqsa mosque in occupied East Jerusalem
articles.summary: Far-right minister entered Islam’s third-holiest site alongside settlers under protection of Israeli occupation forces.
articles.body:
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, performing prayers and appearing to call for a Jewish temple to be located on the site.

With the protection of Israeli occupation forces, Ben-Gvir entered the compound on Monday, accompanied by several rabbis, settlers and security personnel, and declared plans to alter the historical status quo of Islam’s third-holiest site. The far-right politician has performed such provocative antics several times.

Ben-Gvir performed Talmudic prayers and rituals in the eastern section of the mosque’s courtyards, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

As part of the status quo arrangement in place since 1967, performing prayers is not allowed for non-Muslims, although Jewish people are permitted to visit the compound.

“When I was 14 years old, prayer was forbidden, and anyone who murmured was arrested. Today we see redemption. It is very moving to be with you today, and you are right, we must blow the shofar and bring the prayer incantations, and there must be a temple… a temple… a temple… but little by little”, Ben-Gvir said during the incursion, according to Al Jazeera Arabic’s Elias Karram.

“I am very moved… and you say that we must bring the prayer incantations and blow the shofar [ram’s horn],” the national security minister remarked.

The leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, has stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound several times since taking office in 2022, drawing widespread condemnation .

A regular advocate of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the territories occupied by Israel, Ben-Gvir is part of a growing settler movement that wants to take over the compound and build a Jewish synagogue in place of the Muslim holy site.

This latest incursion comes as tens of thousands of Jews have participated in recent days in Yom Kippur prayers, which last for a full month at the Western Wall, also known as the Wailing Wall, preceding Jewish holidays in September.

The Jerusalem governorate condemned the incursion, describing it as a dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of the mosque’s existing historical and legal status, as well as an attempt to impose new realities at the site and alter its Islamic identity, according to Wafa.

Since 2003, Israeli police have allowed settlers to make daily incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, except on Fridays and Saturdays.

Israel often imposes restrictions on Palestinian worshippers. They prevented Eid al-Fitr prayers at Al-Aqsa this year, allowing only 10,000 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank, home to 3.3 million people, into one of Islam’s holiest sites for the first Friday prayers of Ramadan.

articles.title: In 2020, IShowSpeed had just 1 or 2 viewers; 6 years later, he became the first Black creator to hit 50 million YouTube subscribers
articles.summary: US Streamers News: For a guy now sitting at 60 million YouTube subscribers, IShowSpeed's early numbers sound almost unreal. Darren Watkins Jr. had already created his Yo.
articles.body: For a guy now sitting at 60 million YouTube subscribers, IShowSpeed's early numbers sound almost unreal. Darren Watkins Jr. had already created his YouTube channel in 2016, but the serious streaming grind did not really begin until 2020. Back in Cincinnati, Ohio, during his freshman and sophomore years of high school, he was playing NBA 2K and Fortnite for tiny live audiences. Sometimes, there were only one or two viewers watching. That quiet bedroom phase feels miles away from where the channel stands now. His highly expressive reactions helped change the pace of his growth in 2021, when the audience started climbing at a ridiculous speed. He reached 100,000 subscribers in April that year. By July 2022, the number had jumped to 10 million, turning those nearly empty 2020 streams into the starting point of a much bigger story.The 50 million milestone arrived during IShowSpeed’s Africa tourThe next huge checkpoint came on January 21, 2026. Watkins crossed 50 million YouTube subscribers while celebrating his 21st birthday during the “Speed Does Africa” tour, a 28-day run through 20 countries across the continent.And the setting could not have been more chaotic. He reached the milestone while stuck in heavy traffic in Lagos, Nigeria. Instead of marking it from a quiet room, he stood on top of a car with a birthday cake as a huge crowd of local fans surrounded him.That number also carried a bigger record. Reaching 50 million made Watkins the first Black individual creator in YouTube history to hit that subscriber mark. So the moment was not just another subscriber goal. It became a platform milestone attached to his own journey.From 50 million to 60 million in just monthsThe 50 million mark did not slow the channel down. His 2026 momentum continued through global travel streams and a strong run of football content, pushing the subscriber count even higher during the summer.By August 2026, IShowSpeed had crossed 60 million YouTube subscribers. The growth came after months of travel streams and football-focused videos, giving the channel another major jump during the summer. That means the same creator who once streamed from a Cincinnati bedroom to one or two viewers had added another 10 million subscribers after reaching the historic 50 million mark.The timeline is the wild part. The channel began in 2016, the serious streaming came in 2020, 100,000 subscribers arrived in 2021, and 10 million followed in 2022. Then came 50 million in January 2026 and 60 million by August.His 2020 streams were about NBA 2K and Fortnite, with almost nobody in the chat. Six years later, the scale is completely different. The jump from 50 to 60 million also happened within the same 2026 run. The record now attached to Watkins is no longer about surviving the early stage. It is about becoming the first Black individual creator to reach 50 million, then pushing past 60 million before August 2026 was even over.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1781, a live oak stood beside one of the Revolutionary War’s final major battles; 245 years later, crews are removing old chains that once saved it but are now choking it
articles.summary: US News: Specialist arborists have begun careful restoration work in South Carolina to save a 300-year-old southern live oak that stood near one of the final m.
articles.body: Specialist arborists have begun careful restoration work in South Carolina to save a 300-year-old southern live oak that stood near one of the final major battles of the American Revolutionary War. The huge tree stands at the historic Eutaw Springs battlefield in Orangeburg County. It survived musket fire, artillery attacks and centuries of harsh weather. But support systems added decades ago to hold its split trunk together have now become a danger. Heavy iron chains and steel cables wrapped around the branches have grown into the bark, putting pressure on the tree and blocking the movement of water and nutrients through its living tissue. Crews from SavATree, a specialist tree care company, are carrying out a multi-stage restoration project. The work includes removing the metal, improving the soil around the tree and adding modern, flexible support systems to help extend its life.Old metal supports are now harming the treeThe oak's current problems began after a powerful lightning strike more than 50 years ago damaged its canopy and split its large trunk. To stop the heavy tree from collapsing, landowners installed thick steel cables and iron chains around its main branches. The supports held the damaged limbs together for decades. But as the oak continued to grow, its trunk and branches slowly grew around the metal. The steel has now become tightly embedded in the tree, creating a serious problem. It is putting pressure on the cambium layer, the part of the tree that carries nutrients and other materials between the roots and leaves. "Those cables and chains that saved the tree's life are now unfortunately slowly killing the tree," said Aron Landsaw, a certified arborist with SavATree who is leading the work. "It's basically choking out the bark so it can't pull up nutrients." Arborists are carefully removing metal links that can still be reached. They are also cutting tight cables and other supports to reduce pressure on the branches. "Once we remove the cables, the tree should be able to start pulling up some of those nutrients," Landsaw explained. "And it should thrive." The restoration is expected to take at least a year of intensive treatment. After that, scientists will assess the tree's structure and the health and density of its leaves.Oak stands as a witness to the Eutaw Springs battleThe historic tree stands near the centre of the Eutaw Springs battlefield, where American and British forces fought a major battle on 8 September 1781. American troops under General Nathanael Greene launched a surprise morning attack on British forces led by Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Stewart. Continental soldiers initially pushed through the British camp. British troops later regrouped behind the thick brick walls of a nearby farmhouse, stopping the American advance. Although Stewart's forces held the area by nightfall, heavy British casualties forced them to retreat towards Charleston. The withdrawal effectively ended British control over much of the South Carolina interior just weeks before the siege of Yorktown. "We're really standing at the central point of the Eutaw Springs Battlefield," said Catherine Noyes, Liberty Trail Program director and deputy director of land preservation for the American Battlefield Trust. "The British camp was on this property … all around this tree right behind us." Historical researchers say the oak also provided shade and shelter to soldiers and their horses during the battle and the hot late-summer campaign. "It is a witness tree. It witnessed this battle," said Garrison Marcoux, a historian with the South Carolina Battleground Preservation Trust. "It provided shade to the men and their horses in the intense South Carolina September sun." Marcoux said it is unusual for trees this old to survive in the region, especially after facing severe weather and other environmental pressures over many decades. "It's a living relic," Marcoux said. "It's unbelievable to think about."Restoration begins ahead of 250th anniversaryThe survival of the Eutaw Springs oak is especially significant in South Carolina, where many old trees have been lost to major storms and other natural disasters. Former South Carolina State Parks Director Phil Gaines said extreme weather, including Hurricane Hugo in 1989, destroyed much of the region's historic tree canopy. That has made surviving 300-year-old trees particularly rare. The initial $20,000 restoration project is being funded equally by the American Battlefield Trust and the South Carolina 250 Commission. The work comes as South Carolina prepares events marking the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States. Removing the old metal is only part of the restoration. Tree care crews are also improving the soil around the oak. They are using deep-root aeration, organic treatments and low-pressure liquid fertiliser around the tree's drip line. These measures are intended to reduce soil compaction caused by visitors, machinery and years of use around the battlefield. Specialists are also installing a modern lightning protection system. Copper conductors will run down the trunk to help protect the canopy if the tree is struck again. Restoration teams will check soil moisture and the density of the leaf canopy every three months. The monitoring will help determine whether the oak is recovering and rebuilding its natural system for moving water and nutrients after the damaging metal supports are removed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At 19, Baylee Laine gave up a full softball scholarship and worked two jobs to take in her four younger siblings; after a two-year fight, she adopted them
articles.summary: US News: A 19-year-old softball player gave up a full university sports scholarship and worked two jobs while even sleeping in a legal office, all to gain cust.
articles.body: A 19-year-old softball player gave up a full university sports scholarship and worked two jobs while even sleeping in a legal office, all to gain custody of her four younger siblings after years of family instability. Baylee Laine, now 28, eventually legally adopted all four children when she was 21. Her story recently went viral again after she shared a TikTok video showing the family's journey from foster care to their life together today, as detailed in an exclusive interview with People magazine. Laine's journey towards permanent custody began during her childhood, which was marked by her parents' separation and repeated involvement from Child Protective Services (CPS).Timeline of the sibling adoption journeyAge 8: CPS becomes involved and custody moves to her father.High school senior: Her mother gives birth to twins, and Laine considers leaving on a softball scholarship.Decision: Laine turns down the sports scholarship to stay with her siblings.October 2017, age 19: CPS places all four siblings in Laine's care through a foster arrangement.Age 21: The adoptions are finalised after a two-year court fight to end parental rights.Present, age 28: Laine raises her four adopted siblings alongside her biological daughter.Early family instability leads to a major decisionLaine told People that her parents separated when she was five and divorced soon afterwards.“By the time I was 8, CPS got involved,” Laine told the publication, explaining that her father then took custody of her and her brother.Her mother later had four more children with two other men. Laine often helped care for the younger children during weekend visits, but the home became increasingly unstable.“If I wanted to spend time at my mom's apartment, my dad would let me, but it was mostly because she was having a baby, so I would go and help her with the baby,” she explained to People, adding that her mother would “have these men in and out of the house.”“I would be like, 'I'm out of here.' I'd go back home with my dad, and it would only be for weekends at a time, and then a new man came along,” she recalled.When her mother became pregnant with twins, Laine began struggling with the demands of school sports and helping at home.“I was like, 'I can't keep spending my summers taking care of your kids. I can't keep doing this.' I was a softball player and had a full ride to play softball,” she said. “Then I started panicking. 'What am I going to do with my life if my life basically revolves around helping my mom?' She had twins, and then I took a step back.”During her senior year, Laine planned to accept her sports scholarship and leave the situation behind.“My senior year of high school, I thought, 'I'm not doing this. I'm going to go play softball. I'm going to move out of state and I'm going to get away from all of this.' ”But as her departure got closer, she kept thinking about what would happen to her younger siblings.“These kids are going to be all alone,” she remembers thinking. “Then, I decided I'm going to stay, and if I stay, I'm taking them.”Two-year fight for foster care and custodyLaine gave up her plans to move out of state and enrolled at a local community college.She hired a paralegal to help her deal with the child welfare and family court systems. At the same time, she worked long hours to pay legal costs and support the household.“I was working two jobs. I used all my money, and then all of my teenage friends would donate money to me, and we ended up doing a GoFundMe. Most of it was word of mouth; friends of family and people donated to me,” she told People. “We got close to $10,000, and I fought for two years with a paralegal to basically become a foster parent at 18 and get that approved.”The case required Laine to seek the termination of parental rights involving three biological parents. She had to prove that, despite being very young, she could provide a safe and stable home.During the legal battle, she sometimes slept on the floor of her paralegal's office while collecting documents and preparing for court.On 25 October 2017, child protection officials officially placed the four children in Laine's home. She was 19.“Once we did that, I had to fight all three parents to get their rights taken from them, and for the state to see that clearly I can do this,” Laine explained to People.Raising four children changes her own plansTaking full responsibility for four younger children changed Laine's life almost immediately.At the time, the children included her brother, now 17, a sister, now 14, and twin toddlers, now 12.“The minute they dropped them off to us in October, you're full-time mom mode. There were no breaks,” Laine said. “I wasn't leaving anybody's side. The difference from fostering to adoption wasn't that big of a difference in our day-to-day life, but it was like I could finally breathe. I struggle with this. I feel like I have to do everything perfectly to prove myself.”Balancing community college with childcare eventually became too difficult. The twins were too young to qualify for state-funded preschool, making it harder for Laine to continue her education and play softball.“School also became too much because the twins were too little for the state-funded preschools, so I ended up quitting school,” she recalled. “I did play softball at the school for a little while. Once I hired a paralegal, I stopped playing softball at the college. Then, I ended up dropping out.”Laine relied on her partner at the time, along with state support linked to the foster placements, to meet the family's needs.The emotional pressure was also intense.“There were no emotions, no feelings. I became robotic. I had a job to do,” she explained. “I'm religious, so it was like, 'God has put me here to do this. So if this is my one thing, then this is what I'm going to do.' ”She said helping the children recover from years of instability was difficult.“I was dealing with kids with a very traumatic past. It wasn't this peaceful,” she told People. “They were in my bed with me. They were never leaving my side. We had to take showers together because we could not be separated. It took a while for them to adjust to the fact that we have a comfortable home life now, but it was hard at first.”Adoption brings permanent family securityTwo years after the children were placed with Laine, when she was 21, a court finalised the adoptions.The decision ended state welfare supervision and court-ordered visitation arrangements involving the children.“After the adoption, our life got a little bit smoother because there's not so much of a schedule that we have to go through in the state. With the court dates and the visitation and catering to all the rules, we didn't have to do that anymore,” Laine told People, adding that their biological mother has been incarcerated since 2023. “The fact that we were solidified and we were our own unit and we could walk away from it was the biggest difference.”The family felt an even greater sense of security during the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. Being together at home helped the children understand that no legal or parental dispute would suddenly separate them.“Once COVID hit and we were all stuck at home, that was the most calm we all probably felt, because it was always a scary situation,” she said. “Is someone going to come and take us?”“That has to do with being in the foster care system. Kids are always worried this isn't forever. CPS is going to come pick me up or my parents are going to come pick me up, and they're going to run away with me,” she continued. “Once COVID hit and we were all confined to our house and doing our nightly walks, that is where we felt true peace.”Today, Laine is raising her four adopted siblings alongside her three-year-old biological daughter.After she shared the family's story online, the post received six million views and hundreds of messages from relatives, aunts and grandparents dealing with similar child welfare situations.“I encourage them, 'Stay strong, girl. You can do it.' If I can do it, anybody can do it. But it's a lot,” Laine said. “I've said that to quite a few people, but just the fact that you've had this thought or this feeling, it says more than just the fact that your family life is in some sort of chaos and you feel like you should do something. Having that thought alone, you're already steps ahead.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mexico’s mezcal boom is under threat from organized crime
articles.summary: Mexico’s mezcal success story is at risk of being undermined by threats from violent criminal groups.
articles.body:
In the remote hills of Oaxaca, in southern Mexico, the pungent honey-sweet aroma of roasted agave emanating from traditional wood-fired, open-pit, stone ovens is now recognized as the smell of success. In 2025, Mexico produced 7.7 million bottles of mezcal, in comparison to the production total from 2015.

I recently visited a distillery in the town of Santiago Matatlan in Oaxaca. Now whenever I sip a glass of mezcal, I savor the complex spirit and reflect on the remarkable journey each bottle of Mexico’s most enigmatic elixir makes. From trickling out of a small still in an isolated mountain town in one of the country’s most remote regions, to being packed into the back of a cargo truck and carted up more than 750 miles to the U.S. border.

Unfortunately, Mexico’s mezcal success story is at risk of being undermined by threats from violent criminal groups. Mexico is the world’s highest risk country for violent, in-transit cargo truck hijacking. The roadways that lead from Oaxaca’s mountain towns through central Mexico are now the highest risk logistics pathways in the country.

In September 2024, a truck carrying a shipment of Monte Alban mezcal was hijacked in an armed robbery on the Mexico-Tuxpan highway near the town of Zempoala.

In July 2025, a truck carrying 9,000 bottles of premium agave spirits with an estimated value of $1.3 million was stolen in Guanajuato .

On July 6, a truck carrying 64 tons of bottles of alcohol was taken by hijackers in Hidalgo.

The targeting of shipments of mezcal and tequila is part of a broader trend in Mexico. The organized crime groups that specialize in cargo theft seek out food products and beverages that are easily resold at informal markets.

The state of Oaxaca is not yet a major focal point for hijacking, but shipments of mezcal face increasing risk as they move north through hijacking hotspots including Puebla, Mexico State, Michoacan, Jalisco and Guanajuato.

Private sector analysts now consider the state of Puebla, a crossing point for U.S.-bound bottles of mezcal from Oaxaca, to be the worst hotspot for cargo truck hijacking . Local authorities and residents in small towns in Puebla are colluding with criminal groups to hide stolen merchandise and trucks and impede investigations. A similar dynamic of collusion pervades in other states around Mexico City.

Incidents compiled in the Mexico Cargo Truck Hijacking Data Portal created by my company, Reliance Partners, show that during the first six months of 2026, over 79 percent of all hijackings were recorded in Mexico State and Puebla, two states in central Mexico to the north of Oaxaca.

Despite the danger, the trucks keep coming. Mezcal sales are booming in the U.S., contributing to the trend of an average of 20,000 trucks crossing from Mexico into the U.S. in 2025. The global mezcal market is expected to top $1 billion by the early 2030s. The state of Oaxaca produces around 90 percent of Mexico’s mezcal output.

Unlike tequila, which has mostly shifted towards mass-scale industrial production, the overwhelming majority of Mexico’s mezcal is still produced at tiny, family-owned distilleries using low-tech underground ovens and donkey-pulled milling stones. Mezcal is one of few bright spots for Oaxaca, Mexico’s third poorest state, which received a paltry $5 million in foreign direct investment in 2025 out of the record-breaking $41 billion Mexico netted that year.

Overall, goods worth nearly $1 million are lost to cargo robberies in Mexico every day. According to some estimates, nearly 50 cargo trucks are hijacked every day in Mexico. In June, the Mexican Association of Transport Organizations staged a massive protest to draw attention to the problem of highway robbery on Mexican roadways.

Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum has overseen a drop in overall levels of violence in Mexico during her term in office which started in late 2024. But she has also been slow to investigate allegations that members of her Morena party are colluding with criminal groups. The governor of Oaxaca, Soloman Jara Cruz, as well as the governors of the nearby states of Puebla and Mexico State, are all members of Sheinbaum’s Morena party.

Efforts to break up the criminal groups preying on cargo trucks on highways in these states may also involve investigating politicians from Morena who may be collaborating with and protecting criminals.

Mexico’s mezcal boom is a tremendous success story that hinges on producers in remote mountain towns being able to safely ship their bottles along roadways up to the U.S. The loss of a single truckload of mezcal to cargo theft would be a devastating financial loss for most artisan producers.

Every bottle of craft mezcal needs safe passage to make to the tables and bars at high-end restaurants in the U.S. It would be a shame if Oaxaca’s burgeoning mezcal industry is undermined by a political failure to tackle the problem of breaking up hijacking rings and improving security on Mexico’s remote highways.

Mark Vickers is executive vice president and head of International Logistics at Reliance Partners .
